segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God for them is for their salvation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I bear witness for them that they have zeal for God, but not in accordance with knowledge.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For, not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ is the end of the law, so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks like this:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (that is, to bring Christ down)

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: or,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Who will go down into the abyss?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But what does it say?

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because if you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is with the heart that one believes, leading to righteousness, and with the mouth that one declares, leading to salvation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the scripture says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: How, then, are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one they have not heard? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? As it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But not all obeyed the good news. For Isaiah says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Lord, who has believed what they heard from us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I ask, did they not hear? Indeed they did:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I ask, did Israel not know? First Moses says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will make you jealous over what is no nation; over a nation without understanding I will make you angry.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Isaiah is bold enough to say,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I showed myself to those who were not asking for me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But about Israel he says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and defiant people.”

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul’s congregations included both. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones render it as here.

notes.traditional: the righteousness of God; God’s righteousness
notes.note: The phrase can mean the right standing that God gives, God’s own uprightness, or God’s action to set things right; the Greek does not decide, and scholars are divided. The contrast with “their own” suggests a standing that comes from God, but the other senses are not excluded. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify), so the same word could be rendered “justice”.

The Greek word can mean a termination or a goal and outcome. Some interpreters hold that Christ brings the law’s role to a close, others that he is what the law was aiming at, and many that both are intended. “End” is kept because the English word can carry both senses.

notes.phrase: the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it
notes.traditional: Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does these things will live by them
notes.note: Manuscripts differ over where the word “that” stands and over the wording that follows. The reading translated here, adopted by SBLGNT, makes the sentence a paraphrase; the other reading gives a nearly direct quotation of Leviticus 18:5. On either reading Leviticus 18:5 is the passage in view.

notes.phrase: Do not say in your heart
notes.note: Verses 6 to 8 adapt Deuteronomy 30:12–14, with an opening phrase from Deuteronomy 9:4. There Moses says that God’s commandment is not far off in heaven or beyond the sea but near at hand. Paul gives the words to a personified “righteousness that comes from faith”, applies each line to Christ, and has “the abyss” where Deuteronomy has the sea.

The verb means to acknowledge or state something openly, often in a public or binding setting. “Confess” is the traditional rendering and is still used by most translations, but in current English it mainly suggests admitting guilt, which is not in view here. Some modern versions likewise use “declare” or “acknowledge”.

notes.traditional: that Jesus is Lord; the Lord Jesus
notes.note: The Greek is simply “Lord Jesus” as the object of the verb. Most interpreters take it as the content of the declaration, “Jesus is Lord”, which appears elsewhere in Paul as an early Christian acclamation. Some older translations render it “confess the Lord Jesus”.

The quotation is from Joel 2:32 (3:5 in the Greek version), where “the Lord” stands for the personal name of Israel’s God. The surrounding verses, with “Jesus is Lord” and “the same Lord is Lord of all”, indicate that Paul applies the line to Jesus. Most interpreters read it this way.

notes.traditional: of whom they have not heard
notes.note: The Greek construction normally means hearing a person speak, not hearing about a person. On that reading Christ himself is heard in the proclamation of those who are sent. Many translations keep “of whom they have not heard”, which is possible; many commentators prefer the direct sense adopted here.

The noun belongs to the same word-family as “bring good news” in the line from Isaiah just quoted in verse 15, and Paul is drawing on that link. “Gospel” is the standard rendering and means the same thing, but it hides the connection.

notes.traditional: our report; our message (and in verse 17, “faith comes by hearing”)
notes.note: The Greek noun can mean either the act of hearing or the thing heard, a report. Isaiah’s line uses it in the second sense, and Paul repeats the same word twice in verse 17 to draw his conclusion. Most translations have “message” or “report” here and “hearing” in verse 17; one rendering is kept for both so that the reasoning can be followed.

Many later manuscripts read “the word of God”, which older English versions follow; the earliest witnesses have “of Christ”. The phrase may mean the message about Christ or the word Christ himself speaks; the Greek allows either.

notes.phrase: Their voice has gone out into all the earth
notes.note: The words are from Psalm 19:4 (18:5 in the Greek version), where the voice is that of the heavens declaring God’s glory. Paul borrows them for the spread of the proclamation. Interpreters disagree on whether he means this as proof from Scripture or as a deliberately sweeping way of saying the message has gone out widely.

notes.traditional: those who are not a nation; them that are no people
notes.note: The quotation is from Deuteronomy 32:21. “Nation” here is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually rendered “Gentiles”. Paul hears in the Song of Moses an anticipation of non-Jewish peoples coming to Israel’s God and of Israel being provoked by it.

candidates.reason: The plural address recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translators split between “brothers”, “brothers and sisters” and “friends”; readers will notice if it varies.
“Gospel” versus “good news” is a pervasive choice across the whole New Testament and affects the visible link with the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι.
“Confess” now suggests admitting guilt; the word recurs in the Gospels, the Johannine letters and Hebrews in the sense of open acknowledgment and needs one rendering for that sense.
“Preach” and “proclaim” are both common, and the choice recurs in the Gospels, Acts and the letters; “preach” now suggests a sermon in church.
It also occurs in Luke 8 and Revelation, where translations vary between “abyss”, “the deep” and “bottomless pit”; a reader should be able to see it is one term.
